Spies
SPYZE
n. pl.
From Old French espier, to watch, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: a person sent secretly into an enemy’s camp to inspect their works and ascertain their designs. Scripture records three famous sets of spies, and their reports decide the fate of a generation, a city, and a harlot’s household.

Biblical Definition

The spies of Scripture are sent three times to memorable effect. At Kadeshbarnea God commands it: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them (Numbers 13:2). Twelve rulers went; ten came back with the fruit in their hands and this conclusion: We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we (Numbers 13:31). The land was as good as reported and the giants were as real as reported; the difference between the ten and the two was the clause about God, and a nation died in the wilderness over it. Forty years later Joshua, who had been one of the two, sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho (Joshua 2:1) — and this time the report is that the inhabitants’ hearts had melted. Rahab hid them, made her confession, and hung the scarlet line, and Hebrews puts her among the faithful because she had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31). The third set is Moses’ sons of Israel remembering: the men that Moses sent to spy out the land… died by the plague before the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SPY as a person sent into an enemy’s camp to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs, and communicate intelligence; and, in a secondary sense, one who watches the conduct of others.

expand to see more

SPY, n. — A person sent into an enemy’s camp or country to inspect their works, ascertain their strength and designs, and communicate such intelligence.

One who watches the conduct of others — used in a bad sense of a secret and malicious observer.

SPY, v.t. — To gain sight of; to discover at a distance or in concealment; to explore; to view or examine secretly.

Joseph accuses his brethren of being spies three times in Genesis 42, using the charge as a means of testing them.

Galatians 2:4 speaks of false brethren brought in privily, who came in privily to spy out our liberty — the bad sense Webster records.

Key Scripture

Numbers 13:2 — "Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them."

Numbers 13:31 — "But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we."

Numbers 13:33 — "And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight."

Hebrews 11:31 — "By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace."

Numbers 14:11 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, How long will this people provoke me? and how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them?"

Modern Corruption

The report of the ten spies is usually filed under pessimism or poor morale, and Scripture files it under unbelief — a distinction that changes both the diagnosis and the cure.

expand to see more

The ten did not lie about the land or the giants. Their facts were the same facts Caleb and Joshua had, and their conclusion, considered as military assessment, was correct: Israel could not take those cities. The error was in the frame. We be not able is a true sentence in a universe with no God in it, and God’s own verdict on the episode names what was missing: how long will it be ere they believe me, for all the signs which I have shewed among them? Unbelief is not usually a denial of evidence; it is the omission of God from an otherwise accurate calculation. The pastoral consequence is considerable, because the standard modern remedies for discouragement — better morale, positive framing, confidence-building — address the symptom and leave the omission in place.

Rahab supplies the counter-case, and it is the more remarkable for who she was. A Canaanite harlot in a doomed city had heard the same reports the spies brought back forty years earlier — the Red Sea, Sihon, Og — and drew the opposite conclusion: the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath. She acted on it at the risk of her life, hid the men, and hung out the scarlet line, and she is named in Hebrews 11, in James 2, and in the genealogy of Christ. The same evidence produced a generation of carcases in the wilderness and one converted household inside the walls. What made the difference was faith, and faith is a gift.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ragal (H7270), to go about on foot, to spy out, from regel, a foot; tur (H8446), to search out, at Numbers 13:2; Greek kataskopos (G2685) at Hebrews 11:31.

expand to see more

Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to spy out, to go about as a footman or slanderer; Joshua 2:1, Genesis 42:9.

Hebrew tur (H8446) — to search out, to explore; the verb of Numbers 13:2, and of the Preacher searching out wisdom.

Hebrew regel (H7272) — a foot; the root of ragal, since a spy goes on foot.

Greek kataskopos (G2685) — a spy, a scout; a hapax legomenon at Hebrews 11:31.

Greek kataskopeo (G2684) — to spy out; Galatians 2:4, of false brethren spying out Christian liberty.

Usage

"Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:2) — a mission God Himself commanded."

"We be not able to go up… for they are stronger than we (Numbers 13:31) — accurate arithmetic with God left out."

"She had received the spies with peace (Hebrews 11:31) — a Canaanite’s faith commended in the roll of the faithful."
